summary: OpenManus funnels every LLM call through one class: app/llm.py's LLM builds a single client per [llm.*] config name (AsyncOpenAI, AsyncAzureOpenAI, or the hand-rolled BedrockClient) and ask / ask_with_images / ask_tool are the only callers. So the migration is one change: that AsyncOpenAI client is now passed through router_runtime.wrap_openai(), which puts an httpx transport underneath it and sends Chat Completions requests to Router's /v1/responses when Router can serve the model, leaving everything else on the configured provider. All five call sites route: verified against the simulator (5/5 valid requests) and against the real Router (5/5 200, provider=openai), covering non-streaming, streaming, tool calls and images. The suite still passes 4/4, unchanged from the baseline, and nothing happens at all until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set (ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again). Three call paths stay on their provider and are written up below: Azure deployments (the runtime leaves Azure clients alone), the two boto3 Bedrock converse calls in app/bedrock.py, and one the scanner never saw -- app/tool/chart_visualization spawns a node subprocess whose VMind library POSTs to <base_url>/chat/completions with axios, which neither runtime can intercept. Deployments configured against Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint -- which is what the shipped config.example.toml does -- also stay on Anthropic until the host unlock on branch router-migrate/improve/anthropic-compat-host is approved, because that swaps the model Router answers with.
reviewed: I read app/llm.py, app/bedrock.py, app/config.py and the agent/flow callers to see what the traffic actually looks like (a ToolCallAgent loop of up to 20 steps that resends the same system prompt and 40-odd tool schemas every step, plus a growing history), then went through the Router lever table against that shape and measured the candidates live where a measurement was possible. Four are built and tested on branches: prompt caching (measured: a repeated 3.5k-token agent prefix cached 3,328 tokens and cost 47% less per step, where without prompt_cache_key Router cached nothing at all), a retry predicate that no longer resends requests the provider already rejected (measured: 6 Router requests and ~13s became 1 request and 1.4s for one bad payload), per-agent spend labels, and the Anthropic-compat host unlock that makes the shipped default configuration route. Four more are proposed but not built, each because the right value depends on a deployment the repo does not contain: a fallback list for the agent loop (it forfeits the Flex discount, measured at -50% on gpt-5.4-mini, and can change model mid-run), provider_timeout for the two entry points that have no timeout at all, porting the Bedrock branch onto Router with a BYOK credential, and routing the chart tool's axios traffic. Flex itself I left alone: cost-efficient routing is already the account default and the bulk of the traffic (ask_tool) is non-streamed background work it suits. I also considered porting the whole LLM layer from Chat Completions to Responses and rejected it: the translation layer costs nothing measurable, router.policy.json already gives the same levers, and the Azure, Ollama and Bedrock paths would still need Chat Completions.

items.title: Route the shared OpenAI client through Router
items.summary: app/llm.py's AsyncOpenAI client goes through router_runtime.wrap_openai(), so all five chat.completions call sites route to Router's /v1/responses when it can serve the model.
items.gains: Every LLM call the app makes through the OpenAI SDK -- the agent tool loop, the planning flow, the vision path, streamed and buffered -- goes out on one Router key, with per-request spend records and a feature label, and the model becomes a Router catalog choice instead of a provider choice. The request shape the app builds is untouched, and if Router refuses a request before generating, the runtime sends the original request to the configured provider once.
items.price: no change by itself: the same model at Router's catalog price. Cost changes only through the improvements below (prompt caching measured -47% per agent step).
items.why: Everything funnels through one client construction, so one wrap covers the whole application; the runtime decides per request, so Azure, Bedrock, non-catalog models, beta headers and anything else Router cannot serve keep working exactly as before. Pointing the client's base_url at Router instead would have broken the app outright -- Router serves no /v1/chat/completions -- and would have given up the per-request provider fallback.

evidence.detail: 4 passed, same as the recorded baseline (4 passed, 0 failed); compileall clean

check --run on a probe driving ask(stream=False), ask(stream=True), ask_tool and ask_with_images (buffered and streamed): 5 requests reached router-sim, 5 valid, 0 invalid, features app/llm.py:ask / :ask_tool / :ask_with_images

the same probe with check --run --live: 5 requests to Router, 5 ok (200, provider=openai, model=gpt-4o-mini); tool calls came back as tool_calls, the streamed call streamed, the image call answered about the image
with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY unset: router_runtime.active() is False and the client keeps httpx's own AsyncHTTPTransport, so the wrap is a true no-op and the app's requests are unchanged

the runtime drops temperature/top_p for catalog models that reject it (Sonnet 5, *-5-5, OpenAI reasoning models), so the app's unconditional temperature=0.0 does not 400 on them; on the provider path the original request still carries it

items.title: Azure OpenAI deployments stay on Azure
items.summary: When api_type = "azure" the client is AsyncAzureOpenAI, and the runtime deliberately leaves Azure clients on their configured deployment endpoint.
items.gains: Azure deployments keep working exactly as they do today, including their deployment routing and data-residency commitments.
items.loses: nothing today: this traffic is not on Router, so it gets no Router spend record, no catalog choice and no levers.
items.why: An Azure request names an Azure deployment id, not a Router catalog id, and it authenticates against the customer's own Azure resource; wrap_openai() returns Azure clients unchanged rather than guessing a mapping. Routing an Azure deployment would mean naming catalog models in config.toml and giving up the Azure resource, which is a tenancy decision, not a migration step.

evidence.detail: app/llm.py:224 constructs AsyncAzureOpenAI; router_runtime.wrap_openai()'s _is_openai() excludes AzureOpenAI/AsyncAzureOpenAI, so the wrap is a no-op for that branch

items.title: The Bedrock branch stays on boto3
items.summary: With api_type = "aws" the app talks to bedrock-runtime through boto3's converse / converse_stream, which Router does not serve.
items.gains: AWS-only deployments keep working, with their IAM auth and their VPC endpoints.
items.loses: this traffic is not on Router: no Router spend record, no catalog, no levers, and app/bedrock.py keeps hand-translating Bedrock responses into OpenAI shapes.
items.why: Router has no Bedrock converse endpoint, the vendored runtime only sits under httpx-based SDKs (boto3 is neither), and the Bedrock catalog ids Router does list need the caller's own AWS credential registered with Router (requires_byok). Item i6 proposes the port.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all: both sites report "kept: other SDK / endpoint; Router does not serve this vendor's endpoint with the shared key"

items.title: The chart tool's node subprocess stays on the provider
items.summary: app/tool/chart_visualization spawns `npx ts-node src/chartVisualize.ts`, which hands VMind the app's base_url/model/api_key; VMind POSTs <base_url>/chat/completions with axios, and nothing in that path can be routed as it stands.
items.gains: the chart tool keeps working unchanged.
items.loses: this is real production LLM traffic, paid for with the provider key, that is not on Router: no spend record, no label, no catalog choice. It is also traffic the scanner never reported, so it would have gone unnoticed.
items.why: Router serves no /v1/chat/completions, so pointing VMind at Router 404s. The vendored TypeScript runtime routes by wrapping fetch, and VMind 2.0.5 uses axios, which in node does not go through fetch; VMind exposes a url and headers, not a transport. Routing it means changing where that LLM call is made (item i7), and the subprocess's dev dependencies are not installed in this environment, so no change there could be tested here.

evidence.detail: app/tool/chart_visualization/data_visualization.py:228 passes {base_url, model, api_key} to the subprocess; chartVisualize.ts:341-347 builds `new VMind({url: `${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, headers: {...apiKey}})`; `npm view @visactor/vmind@2.0.5 dependencies` lists axios ^1.4.0

items.title: Browser Use CLI runs its own LLM out of process
items.summary: app/agent/manus.py launches `uvx browser-use --cli-mcp` as an MCP server with BROWSER_USE_API_KEY and talks to it over stdio; whatever model that process uses is billed on its own account, not through this app's client.
items.loses: nothing this migration could have taken: no LLM request is built in this repository for that traffic.
items.why: It is a separate product invoked as a subprocess with its own credential and its own endpoint. Putting it on Router would mean configuring Browser Use, not changing this codebase. Flagged so the spend is not assumed to be fully covered by the Router key.

evidence.detail: app/agent/manus.py:18-38 and :85-96 (command uvx browser-use --cli-mcp, env BROWSER_USE_API_KEY / BROWSER_USE_CLOUD_API_URL); OPENMANUS_DISABLE_BROWSER_USE=1 disables it

items.title: Cache the agent loop's stable prompt prefix
items.summary: router.policy.json sets prompt_cache_key to each request's feature label, so Router caches the system prompt and tool schemas an agent step resends every turn.
items.gains: Measured live through the app's own client on a two-step agent-shaped loop (gpt-4o-mini, ~3.5k-token stable prefix): with the policy, step 2 cached 3,328 of 3,483 prompt tokens and cost $0.000289; without it, 0 cached and $0.000545 -- 47% off that step, and the saving grows with the history an OpenManus run accumulates over its 20 steps. Cached input reads at the catalog's cache_read_input rate (claude-sonnet-5: $0.20 instead of $2 per 1M).
items.loses: nothing measurable: Router-bound requests only, the provider path is untouched, and the runtime already set this key by itself for Claude. It only helps when a prefix repeats above the provider's ~1,024-token minimum, so short one-shot calls see no change.
items.price: cheaper: -47% on a measured repeated agent step; no change to anything that does not repeat a prefix
items.why: This is the shape of the traffic. A ToolCallAgent step resends the same system prompt and the same tool schemas every turn, and before this the app sent no cache key at all for OpenAI or open-weight models -- and measured on this account, gpt-4o-mini cached nothing without one. One committed policy file, no code change, reversible by deleting it.

evidence.detail: A/B through app/llm.py's wrapped client: policy on -> step 2 cached=3328/3483, cost $0.000289; ROUTER_MIGRATE_POLICY=off -> step 2 cached=0/3523, cost $0.000545. A standalone /v1/responses A/B agreed (3,328 cached, $0.00027 vs $0.00052)
the compiled policy puts prompt_cache_key='app/llm.py:ask_tool' on the planned Router body for an ask_tool-shaped request; check --run still 5/5 valid
4 passed on the branch

items.title: Stop retrying requests the provider already rejected
items.summary: All three entry points retried on bare `Exception` six times with up to 60s of backoff; is_retryable() keeps that only for timeouts, connection errors, 408/409/429 and 5xx.
items.gains: Measured live on the same rejected request (a bad image payload, gpt-4o-mini through Router): 6 Router requests and a RetryError after ~13s became 1 request and a clean error after 1.4s. Behind a shared gateway that is 6x the request count, 6x the spend-cap pressure and a minute of wall clock for an answer that cannot change; it also fixes the file's own stated intent -- TokenLimitExceeded was being retried six times despite the comment saying it should not be.
items.loses: A rejected request is no longer sent again, so a provider 4xx that would have succeeded on a retry (a transient 400 from an overloaded edge, say) now surfaces to the caller on the first attempt. Everything the app's callers already handle as a failure still arrives as the same exception type.
items.price: cheaper on failure paths (up to 6x fewer requests per rejected call); no change on success
items.why: An autonomous agent that loops 20 times multiplies every retry policy by its step count, and a Router key has a spend cap that is enforced after usage is recorded, so retry storms are exactly what you do not want in front of a gateway. This also composes with Router's error surface: a Router timeout is a 504 and a rate limit is a 429, both of which stay retryable.

evidence.detail: before (migration branch): 6x 400 /v1/responses for one bad image, RetryError after ~13s. after (this branch): 1x 400, AuthenticationError after 1.4s (the 401 is the dummy provider key in the check sandbox, i.e. the runtime's single provider retry, unchanged)
classification probe: TokenLimitExceeded, 400, 401 -> not retried; 429, 500, 504, APITimeoutError and the ValueError the streaming paths raise on an empty response -> retried
4 passed on the branch

items.title: Label LLM requests with the agent that made them
items.summary: LLM.feature_headers() sends "<config name>:<entry point>" in the header the runtime reads, so Router's spend records name the Manus agent, the planning flow, the vision config or the chart tool instead of a source line.
items.gains: Spend becomes attributable per agent and flow -- the thing a CTO actually asks about when an autonomous agent product's bill moves -- and router.policy.json can then target one agent (its `features` keys match these labels), e.g. a cheaper model or its own timeout for the vision config. It also makes i1's cache key per agent, which is what the cached prefix actually depends on.
items.loses: The automatic label (app/llm.py:ask_tool and friends) is replaced, so Router request tags no longer name the source line; any policy entry or dashboard filter written against the old labels has to be rewritten against the new ones. Requests made with a caller-supplied extra_headers keep the caller's value.
items.why: Every agent and flow in OpenManus already runs under its own [llm.*] config name, and the class already knows it -- but it threw that away, so all traffic from all agents landed under three labels. Three lines of plumbing turn the existing config structure into spend attribution and policy granularity.

evidence.detail: 5 of 5 calls 200, labelled probe_nostream:ask, probe_stream:ask, probe_tool:ask_tool, probe_img:ask_with_images, probe_img_stream:ask_with_images (in a real run: manus:ask_tool, vision:ask_with_images, default:ask ...)
check --run: 5/5 valid with the new feature labels
4 passed on the branch

items.title: Route the Anthropic-compatible endpoint the shipped config uses
items.summary: Unlocks api.anthropic.com on the app's client and maps the dated Claude id the shipped config names to claude-sonnet-5, so the default OpenManus configuration routes instead of staying on Anthropic.
items.gains: The configuration this project actually ships -- config.example.toml and config.example-model-anthropic.toml both point the OpenAI SDK at https://api.anthropic.com/v1/ with a dated 3.7 Sonnet id -- is the one case where the migration otherwise changes nothing at all. With this, those deployments route with no config edit: verified live, 3 of 3 calls 200 from provider=anthropic as claude-sonnet-5, streaming and tool calls included. Sonnet 5 is also $2/$10 per 1M against 3.7 Sonnet's $3/$15 list.
items.loses: Router answers with Claude Sonnet 5 where the config asked for Claude 3.7 Sonnet: a different, newer model, so answers change, and prompts tuned for 3.7 Sonnet may behave differently. temperature is dropped on those requests because Sonnet 5 does not accept it (the app sends 0.0 unconditionally, so the model's own default applies instead). Requests Router refuses still go to Anthropic with the original dated id, so the provider path keeps its exact behaviour.
items.price: cheaper per token ($2/$10 vs $3/$15 per 1M list), plus i1's caching, but a different model is answering
items.why: Without it the headline result is misleading: the default deployment's traffic would not be on Router at all. With it, the change is a product decision -- which model answers -- so it belongs in front of a human rather than inside the migration commit.

evidence.detail: probe with base_url=https://api.anthropic.com/v1/ and model=claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219: 3 requests, 3 ok, 200 /v1/responses model=claude-sonnet-5 provider=anthropic (ask buffered, ask streamed, ask_tool returning a tool call)
check --run on the same probe: 3 valid Router requests, model rewritten to claude-sonnet-5
4 passed on the branch
the image path fails on this config for an unrelated pre-existing reason: app/llm.py's MULTIMODAL_MODELS whitelist does not list any 3.7 Sonnet id, so ask_with_images raises before any request

items.title: Give the agent loop a fallback model
items.summary: Add a `fallbacks` list to router.policy.json for the tool-loop label so a step that the primary model's provider cannot serve is answered by a second catalog model instead of failing the run.
items.gains: A 20-step agent run currently dies on a provider outage: the retry predicate backs off and gives up, and the whole task is lost along with the spend already incurred on the earlier steps. Router falls through a missing model, a model this key may not use and an invalid parameter silently, cross-vendor (measured upstream: gpt-5-nano to claude-haiku-4-5).
items.loses: A different model can answer a step mid-run, which for an agent means a different tool-calling style inside one conversation, and the least capable candidate caps the tools, structured output, modalities and context of every request on that label. Fallbacks also forfeit Flex (allow_flex_tier is dropped when a list applies; Flex measured -50% on gpt-5.4-mini), and there is no fallback once a stream has started, so the streamed paths gain nothing. Truncated attempts are still billed.
items.price: the serving candidate's price when it serves; on Flex-eligible OpenAI models the loop gives up the Flex discount
items.why: Proposed rather than built because the candidate list only makes sense against a deployment's own model choice, which this repository does not contain -- a committed list of ids would be wrong for most installs. My recommendation: scope it to the *:ask_tool label only (leave the streamed, user-facing call on Flex), and pick a candidate of comparable tool-calling ability rather than a cheap one, since a weak fallback breaks the loop it is meant to rescue.

items.title: Serve the Bedrock deployments through Router
items.summary: Retire app/bedrock.py's hand-written converse translation and let api_type = "aws" use the same wrapped OpenAI client against Router's Bedrock catalog ids with a BYOK credential.
items.gains: Deletes 334 lines of bespoke protocol translation that today only handles one tool call per turn and tracks tool-use ids in a module-level global (app/bedrock.py's CURRENT_TOOLUSE_ID, with a "Tmp solution" comment), and puts AWS-shaped deployments on the same spend records, labels, caching and levers as everything else. Router lists the ids these deployments use (us.anthropic.claude-*, global.anthropic.*).
items.loses: Those Bedrock ids are requires_byok: without the caller's AWS credential registered on Router the requests 403, so this cannot ship without an account change. An AWS-only deployment also gains a dependency on Router's reachability where today it talks to a VPC endpoint under its own IAM, and the streaming and tool-call behaviour would come from the translation layer instead of its own code, so output can differ.
items.price: Bedrock catalog ids run about 10% above the Anthropic-served equivalents through Router (us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 $2.2/$11 vs claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10 per 1M); a deployment with no AWS requirement would be cheaper still on the Anthropic ids.
items.why: Proposed, not built: it needs a provider credential on the Router account and a deployment to test against, and the code it replaces is the only path for customers who must stay inside AWS. Worth doing when a BYOK credential exists -- the translation layer it deletes is the most fragile code in the LLM path.

items.title: Route the chart tool's LLM call
items.summary: Move the VMind chart call off its own axios request to <base_url>/chat/completions so that traffic lands on Router too.
items.gains: Closes the last hole in the migration: today this is the only LLM request the app pays for that no Router key sees, and it carries the provider key into a node subprocess. On Router it would get the same spend record, label, model catalog and caching as the rest.
items.loses: Either the chart prompt flow moves into the Python side and VMind is used only for rendering -- a rewrite of a third-party integration whose prompt engineering is what produces usable chart specs -- or an axios adapter shim has to be vendored into chartVisualize.ts, which puts a translation layer inside a dependency's HTTP path. Neither could be tested here: the subprocess's node dependencies are not installed in this environment.
items.price: unchanged per token; the traffic becomes visible and cacheable
items.why: Proposed, not built, precisely because it cannot be verified here and a blind edit to an untestable subprocess is how a working feature silently breaks. The cheap first step is the smaller one: have the Python side pass a Router catalog model id and a label, so that when the call is eventually routed it is already labelled.

items.title: Put a timeout on the two entry points that have none
items.summary: Add provider_timeout to router.policy.json for the ask and ask_with_images labels, which pass no timeout to the SDK at all (only ask_tool does, at 300s).
items.gains: A hung provider call currently stalls an agent run indefinitely on those two paths; a server-side cap turns it into a 504 the app's retry can act on (and after i2 a 504 is still retried, which is the right behaviour). Router accepts 1-660 seconds.
items.loses: A long legitimate generation that would have finished after the cap is cut off and retried, which costs the tokens of the truncated attempt. The right number depends on the deployment's model and max_tokens.
items.price: a small risk of paying twice for a slow-but-valid generation; otherwise no change
items.why: Proposed rather than built because picking the number without a production latency distribution is guesswork, and too low a value turns healthy slow calls into retries. My recommendation: 120s for the two unprotected labels, left off ask_tool, which already has its own 300s SDK timeout.

items.title: Put a spend cap on the Router key for this app
items.summary: An account-side setting, not code: give each OpenManus deployment's Router key a spend cap, because the app is an autonomous loop that can spend without a human in the loop.
items.gains: OpenManus runs up to 20 model steps per task with a growing prompt and no cost ceiling of its own; max_input_tokens is optional in config and unset in every shipped example. A per-key cap is the only thing between a runaway task and the bill. A capped key returns 401, which after i2 fails fast instead of being retried six times.
items.loses: A deployment that hits its cap stops serving until the cap is raised, and Router's caps are applied after usage is recorded, so concurrent requests can overshoot slightly.
items.price: no change to unit price; it bounds the total
items.why: This is the decision I would most want a human to make before this traffic grows: the levers are on app.router.com (per-key spend cap, and while you are there, confirm the cost-efficient-routing default that the migration inherits), so no commit can carry it. Decide the cap per deployment and set it on the key you issue for each.

evidence.detail: config/config.example*.toml set no max_input_tokens, so the app's own token guard is inactive by default; a Router key locked by its cap answers 401
